question: Moti Masjid in Agra fort was constructed by which of the following Mughal Emperors?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Shahjahan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Shahjahan:**

 
 
• Shahjahan reigned during the peak of Mughal architectural splendor.
 
• He commissioned the Moti Masjid (Pearl Mosque) within the Agra Fort, known for its pristine white marble construction.
 
• His most iconic creation is the Taj Mahal, a testament to his love for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
 
• He also significantly redesigned the Agra Fort, adding numerous marble structures.
 
• Shahjahan built the Jama Masjid in Delhi, another architectural masterpiece.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Aurangzeb:**

 
 
• Aurangzeb's reign saw a decline in Mughal architectural patronage.
 
• While he did construct the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, his focus shifted more towards military campaigns and expanding the empire.
 
• His architectural style was less ornate than that of Shah Jahan.
 
• Aurangzeb's rule is often characterized by its strict adherence to Islamic law.
 
• His rule expanded the Mughal empires territory to its largest size.
 
 
 
• **Jahangir:**
 
 
• Jahangir was known for his love of art and gardens.
 
• He continued the construction of Akbar's tomb in Sikandra.
 
• He significantly contributed to the development of Mughal painting.
 
• Jahangir also designed many beautiful gardens.
 
• His rule was known for relative peace, and prosperity.
 
 
 
• **Akbar:**
 
 
• Akbar's architectural style blended Persian and Indian influences.
 
• He built the Agra Fort, although Shahjahan later modified it extensively.
 
• He also constructed the city of Fatehpur Sikri, including the Buland Darwaza and Panch Mahal.
 
• He was known for his religious tolerance.
 
• Akbar's rule consolidated the Mughal Empire.
